summary: Specifies the Internet Storage Name Service (iSNS), a protocol that helps iSNS clients and servers discover, manage and configure iSCSI and Fibre Channel devices on an IP network. It provides discovery services comparable to those in Fibre Channel networks. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: iSNS is a name and discovery service for storage devices on an IP network. Storage devices register themselves with an iSNS server, which keeps a database of who is there and where. Other devices query that database to find targets, and the server can also send notifications when the set of devices changes. The RFC also defines how to partition the devices into groups and how to map Fibre Channel devices onto iSCSI ones.

questions: how do iscsi devices discover each other
what is an isns discovery domain
what is the internet storage name service
subtitle: A name and discovery service that lets storage devices on an IP network find and manage each other.

tldr.problem: Storage devices normally need to be told about each other one at a time, so an administrator has to configure every device by hand with its own list of known initiators and targets.
tldr.mechanism: Devices register their attributes with an iSNS server over the iSNS protocol. The server keeps the database, answers queries about other devices, groups devices into discovery domains and sends state change notifications when the set of devices changes.
tldr.outcome: The server becomes a single configuration point for a storage network that mixes iSCSI and Fibre Channel devices, and the RFC defines the message format, the object model, the security requirements and the registries needed to run it.

facts.value: 12 bytes, plus N bytes of payload and L bytes of authentication block

facts.label: Attribute format
facts.value: Tag, Length and Value, 8 bytes plus the value, padded to a 4-byte boundary

facts.label: PDUs per message
facts.value: Up to 65536, the limit of the two-byte Sequence ID

facts.label: Object model
facts.value: Network Entity, Portal, Storage Node, Portal Group, FC Device, Discovery Domain, Discovery Domain Set

facts.value: OPTIONAL for iSCSI and REQUIRED for iFCP

today: RFC 4171 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2005, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of the Internet Storage Name Service protocol, its object model and its security requirements.

sections.title: One Server Instead of Device-by-Device Setup
sections.content:
iSNS facilitates scalable configuration and management of iSCSI and Fibre Channel storage devices in an IP network by providing a set of services comparable to that available in Fibre Channel networks. It allows the administrator to go beyond a simple device-by-device management model, where each storage device is manually and individually configured with its own list of known initiators and targets. Using iSNS, each storage device subordinates its discovery and management responsibilities to the iSNS server, which thereby serves as the consolidated configuration point through which management stations can configure and manage the entire storage network, including both iSCSI and Fibre Channel devices.

An iSNS implementation MAY provide support for one or both of iSCSI and iFCP. Use of iSNS is OPTIONAL for iSCSI and REQUIRED for iFCP. This document focuses on the interaction between iSNS servers and iSNS clients; interactions among multiple authoritative primary iSNS servers are a potential topic for future work.
sections.plainLanguage: Storage networks usually need every device to know about every other device, which means configuring each one by hand. iSNS replaces that with one server that holds the list. A device registers itself and its attributes with the server, and the server becomes the single place where the whole storage network is configured.

sections.title: The Four Pieces of the Service
sections.content:
The iSNS Protocol (iSNSP) is a flexible and lightweight protocol that specifies how iSNS clients and servers communicate. It is suitable for various platforms, including switches and targets as well as server hosts.

An iSNS client is a process co-resident in the storage device. It initiates transactions with iSNS servers, registers device attribute information, downloads information about other registered clients in a common Discovery Domain, and receives asynchronous notification of events that occur in its DDs. Management stations are a special type of iSNS client that have access to all DDs stored in the iSNS.

An iSNS server responds to iSNS protocol queries and requests and initiates State Change Notifications. Properly authenticated information submitted by a registration request is stored in the iSNS database. The iSNS database is the information repository for the server or servers, maintaining information about iSNS client attributes. A directory-enabled implementation of iSNS may store client attributes in an LDAP directory infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Four pieces make up the service. The iSNS protocol is the message format clients and servers speak. A client is a process inside a storage device that registers the device, looks up other devices and receives notifications. A server answers those requests and keeps the database. The database is the repository of client attributes, and a directory-enabled implementation may keep it in an LDAP directory.

sections.title: The Four Services
sections.content:
There are four main functions of iSNS.

The name service lets all entities in a storage network register in and query the iSNS database. Both targets and initiators can register, as well as query for information about other initiators and targets, so a client initiator can obtain information about target devices. This service is modelled on the Fibre Channel Generic Services Name Server described in FC-GS-4, with extensions, operating within the context of an IP network.

The Discovery Domain and Login Control service partitions Storage Nodes into more manageable groupings for administrative and login control purposes. Storage Nodes must be in at least one common enabled DD in order to obtain information about each other, and devices can be members of multiple DDs simultaneously. Login Control allows targets to delegate their access control and authorization policies to the iSNS server: the target node or device downloads the list of authorized initiators from the iSNS, and only initiators that match the identification and authorization provided by the iSNS are allowed access by that target during session establishment. Placing Portals of a Network Entity into Discovery Domains indicates the preferred IP Portal interface through which storage traffic should access specific Storage Nodes.

The State Change Notification service allows the server to issue notifications about network events that affect the operational state of Storage Nodes. Regular registrations are controlled by the Discovery Domain service, so receipt of regular SCNs is limited to the domains in which the triggering event takes place. Management registrations can only be requested by Control Nodes, and the resulting management SCNs are not bound by the Discovery Domain service. If resources are exhausted, the server MAY refuse SCN service by returning an SCN Registration Rejected, status code 17.

The open mapping stores naming and discovery information about both Fibre Channel and iSCSI devices, so the server can hold a mapping of a Fibre Channel device to a proxy iSCSI device in the IP network, and mappings of an iSCSI device to a proxy WWN. Storing the mapping in the server makes it open to any authorized iSNS client, instead of hiding it inside a gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: The service does four things. It is a name service, so a device can look up the targets it may talk to. It groups devices into discovery domains, so a host only learns about the targets it should see and a target can delegate its list of allowed initiators to the server. It sends state change notifications, so a client hears about targets that appear or disappear. And it stores mappings between Fibre Channel devices and iSCSI ones, so the two worlds can be managed together.

sections.title: Finding the Server, and Getting Past NAT
sections.content:
An iSNS client has to find the iSNS server first. Three mechanisms are described. The Service Location Protocol provides a framework for hosts to learn the existence, location and configuration of networked services; a Service Agent can be co-hosted in the iSNS server and a User Agent in each client, and each client multicasts a discovery message that the Service Agent answers. The IP address of the iSNS server can also be stored in a DHCP server and downloaded by clients using a DHCP option. The iSNS heartbeat message lets clients within the broadcast or multicast domain of the server discover the location of the active server and any backup servers.

The iSNS protocol is transport-neutral: query and registration messages are transported over TCP or UDP, and heartbeat messages are transported using IP multicast or broadcast. When UDP is used, each datagram MUST contain exactly one iSNS PDU. For ESI monitoring and SCN delivery over TCP, the server opens the connection to the port the client registered.

NAT affects the information the server holds. If the client is in a different addressing domain from the server, the IP addresses stored in the server may not be correct when interpreted in the client's domain. The RFC describes three approaches: requiring the canonical TCP port and having clients query for the DNS Fully Qualified Domain Name stored in the Entity Identifier field, so that local DNS servers can map it; deploying a distributed network of iSNS servers with one inside and one outside each NAT boundary, sharing updates over LDAP; or running the server so that it exclusively supports clients in the global addressing domain and configuring the NAT gateways so that those clients can start iSNSP sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: A client has to find the server first. It can use the Service Location Protocol, a DHCP option, or the heartbeat message the server sends to the multicast address. The protocol itself runs over TCP or UDP, and the heartbeat goes out over IP multicast or broadcast. If a NAT gateway sits between client and server, the addresses in the database may not match the client's view, and the RFC describes several ways to handle that.

sections.title: The Objects the Database Holds
sections.content:
The iSNS object model provides the elements needed to describe the storage device objects and attributes that may exist on an IP storage network.

The Network Entity object is a container of Storage Node objects and Portal objects, representing the infrastructure supporting access to a unique set of one or more Storage Nodes. Its Entity Identifier attribute is the key used to register it. A single physical device may be represented by more than one logical Network Entity, and a logical entity may be supported by more than one physical device, such as several Fibre Channel to iSCSI gateways bridging one Fibre Channel network.

The Portal object is an interface through which access to Storage Nodes within the Network Entity can be obtained, and is uniquely distinguished by its IP address and TCP/UDP port. The Storage Node object is the logical endpoint of an iSCSI or iFCP session: in iFCP it is represented by the World Wide Port Name, and in iSCSI by the iSCSI Name of the device.

The Portal Group object represents an association between a Portal and an iSCSI Node. The Portal Group Tag, if non-NULL, indicates that the associated Portal provides access to the associated iSCSI Storage Node, and all Portals with the same tag value for that node allow coordinated access to it. An FC Device object holds Fibre Channel information. The Discovery Domain partitions Storage Nodes into groupings for administrative and login control, and a Discovery Domain Set holds a set of Discovery Domains; valid and active DDs belong to at least one active DDS, and DDs that do not belong to an activated DDS are not enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: The database holds seven kinds of object. A Network Entity groups the storage nodes and portals of one piece of infrastructure, keyed by an entity identifier. A Portal is one network interface, keyed by its IP address and port. A Storage Node is the logical endpoint of a session, keyed by its iSCSI name or Fibre Channel port name. A Portal Group says which portal reaches which iSCSI node. An FC Device holds Fibre Channel attributes, and Discovery Domains and Discovery Domain Sets hold the groupings.

sections.title: The Message Format
sections.content:
The iSNSP message format is similar to that of other common protocols such as DHCP, DNS and BOOTP. An iSNSP message may be sent in one or more Protocol Data Units, and each PDU is 4-byte aligned. The header holds the iSNSP VERSION, FUNCTION ID, PDU LENGTH, FLAGS, TRANSACTION ID and SEQUENCE ID, and the payload holds attributes for the operation. A response may add an authentication block, and the total length is 12 plus the payload length plus the authentication block length.

The version described in this document is 0x0001, and all other values are RESERVED. The FUNCTION ID defines the type of message and the operation to be executed: values with the leading bit cleared are query, registration and notification messages, while values with the leading bit set are response messages. All PDUs of one message share the same FUNCTION ID and TRANSACTION ID, and a reply reuses the TRANSACTION ID of its request. The SEQUENCE ID is unique for each PDU within a transaction, starts at zero, and the two-byte field allows up to 65536 PDUs per message.

The payload is of variable length and holds attributes in Tag-Length-Value form: a 4-byte tag, a 4-byte length and the value, for a total of 8 plus the value length. Variable-length values are padded with zero bytes to a 4-byte boundary, and there is no explicit count of the pad bytes. Every response message carries a 4-byte Status Code as the first field of the payload. A code of 0 means Successful, and a non-zero code rejects the entire request message. The codes run from 1 Unknown Error and 2 Message Format Error through 17 SCN Registration Rejected and 18 Attribute Not Implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is one or more protocol data units. The header is 12 bytes: version, function id, length, flags, transaction id and sequence id. The payload holds attributes in tag, length, value form, each padded to a four-byte boundary. Responses carry a status code, where zero means success. A request that is refused is refused as a whole, with one status code for the entire message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The interaction between the iSNS server and its clients is subject to three threats. An attacker could alter iSNS protocol messages, for example to direct iSCSI and iFCP devices to establish connections with rogue peer devices, or to weaken or eliminate IPsec protection. An attacker could masquerade as the real iSNS server using false heartbeat messages, which could cause devices to use rogue servers. An attacker could gain knowledge about the devices by snooping iSNS messages, which could aid a denial-of-service attack or outright theft.

To address these, unicast iSNS messages may need to be authenticated, and confidentiality support is REQUIRED when certain functions of the iSNS server are used. For protecting unicast messages, iSNS servers supporting security MUST implement ESP in tunnel mode and MAY implement transport mode, and all iSNS implementations supporting security MUST support the replay protection mechanisms of IPsec. Multicast messages such as the heartbeat need not be confidential, but client devices MUST support the ability to authenticate broadcast or multicast messages, using the iSNS authentication block, which is identical in format to the SLP authentication block; clients MUST implement it and MUST support BSD value 0x002.

The implementation requirements are strict in places. If the server distributes authorizations between peers, IPsec ESP with the null transform MUST be implemented; if it distributes security policy, authentication, data integrity and confidentiality MUST be supported and used. Conforming implementations MUST support both IKE Main Mode and Aggressive Mode. Manual keying SHOULD NOT be used since it does not provide rekeying support, and conforming implementations MUST support authentication using a pre-shared key.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists three threats: an attacker who rewrites messages to point devices at rogue peers, an attacker who pretends to be the server with fake heartbeat messages, and an attacker who snoops the messages to learn what equipment exists. Unicast messages can be protected with IPsec in tunnel mode, and multicast messages such as the heartbeat must be authenticated with the authentication block. Keying is done with IKE, and manual keying is discouraged because it cannot rekey.

sections.title: The Registries IANA Keeps
sections.content: IANA keeps three registries for this protocol. The first is the registry of Block Storage Protocols, which lists the protocols that can be carried over iSNS. The second is the registry of Standard iSNS Attributes, which holds the attribute tags used in the Tag-Length-Value payload. The third is the Block Structure Descriptor registry, whose values describe the structure of the authentication block used for multicast and broadcast messages, where value 0x002 is the one that MUST be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps three registries for this protocol: the block storage protocols, the standard iSNS attributes and the block structure descriptor values used by the authentication block.

viz.caption: THE iSNSP PROTOCOL DATA UNIT HEADER

fields.name: iSNSP Version
fields.desc: The version described in this document is 0x0001. All other values are RESERVED.

fields.name: Function ID
fields.desc: The type of message and the operation. A cleared leading bit means a request; a set leading bit means a response.

fields.name: PDU Length
fields.desc: Length of the payload in bytes. It must be 4-byte aligned.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bits 16 to 21 say whether the sender is a client or a server, whether an authentication block is present, and whether this is the first or last PDU.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.desc: Unique for each outstanding request. The reply reuses the value of its request.

fields.name: Sequence ID
fields.desc: Unique for each PDU in a transaction, starting at zero. It allows up to 65536 PDUs per message.

items.label: SCN
items.desc: A state change notification generated by the server.

items.label: DevAttrRegRsp
items.desc: Response to a registration request. The leading bit is set on responses.

items.label: Message Format Error
items.desc: The message could not be parsed as an iSNS message.

items.label: Source Unauthorized
items.desc: The source is not allowed to make this request.

items.label: No Such Entry
items.desc: The requested entry does not exist.

items.label: Version Not Supported
items.desc: The iSNSP version is not supported by the server.

items.label: SCN Registration Rejected
items.desc: The server refused the state change notification registration.
